title: Teen summer work has partly rebounded but remains far below its historical role as a routine entry into paid work
source_unit: Pew Research Center analysis of U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics employment data, published August 19, 2026
geography: United States; teens ages 16 to 19, with summer employment, age, race/ethnicity, industry, and occupation comparisons

observations.period: 1948-2026; summer employment among teens ages 16 to 19

denominator.unit: U.S. 16- to 19-year-olds in nonseasonally adjusted federal employment data

summer_2026.unit: percent employed for at least part of summer, averaging June and July 2026

summer_2025.unit: percent employed for at least part of summer, June through August 2025

long_run_context.value: more than half of 16- to 19-year-olds worked for at least part of the summer in most years through 2000, but the rate has remained well below that historical norm since the early 2000s

observations.method: Pew analysis of BLS monthly employment-population ratios; summer averages use June-July-August except 2026, which uses June-July because August data were not yet available.
observations.uncertainty: The 2026 summer comparison is incomplete relative to prior three-month summer averages, and the employment-population ratio does not identify hours, earnings, job quality, or whether work displaced school, care, or leisure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower teen employment may reflect schooling, family resources, changing employer demand, legal constraints, transportation, competition from older workers, or different youth preferences rather than a single loss of work opportunity.

observations.period: June-July 2026; summer employment by race and ethnicity

denominator.unit: U.S. 16- to 19-year-olds in the published race/ethnicity comparison

exposure_gap.value: the published summer employment range spans 18 percentage points between White and Asian teens

observations.method: Pew descriptive analysis of BLS employment data with race and ethnicity categories as published; the source notes that White, Black, and Asian categories include those who are Hispanic, while Hispanic is of any race.
observations.uncertainty: These are descriptive employment-population differences and do not identify the role of household income, local labor demand, transportation, school schedules, discrimination, immigration status, or job-search behavior.
observations.subgroup: White, Hispanic, Black, and Asian teens ages 16 to 19 as defined in the source tables.
observations.counterinterpretation: Group employment differences may reflect different combinations of school, family, geographic, legal, cultural, and labor-market conditions; the percentages do not measure willingness or job quality.

denominator.unit: U.S. 16- to 19-year-olds in the published age comparison

ages_18_19.unit: percent employed during the first two summer months of 2026

ages_16_17.unit: percent employed during the first two summer months of 2026

age_gradient.value: 18- and 19-year-olds were about twice as likely as 16- and 17-year-olds to be employed

life_stage_route.value: access to paid work appears to expand sharply across the transition from younger to older adolescence

observations.method: Descriptive comparison of BLS employment-population ratios for two teen age bands.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison does not separate legal eligibility, transportation, school obligations, employer preferences, prior experience, or local labor-market differences.
observations.counterinterpretation: Older teens may have more legal autonomy, credentials, transportation, and availability; the age gradient does not show that younger teens face a single access barrier.

denominator.unit: employed U.S. 16- to 19-year-olds in the published summer industry comparison

accommodation_food.unit: percent of employed teens in accommodation and food services in summer 2026

retail.unit: percent of employed teens in retail trade in summer 2026

transportation_material_moving.unit: percent of employed teens in transportation and material-moving jobs in summer 2026, up from 9% in 2025

office_admin.unit: percent of employed teens in office and administrative jobs in summer 2026, down from 9% in 2025

first_job_sector.value: hospitality, food service, retail, and logistics remain major institutional entry points into paid work for teenagers

observations.method: Pew analysis of BLS industry and occupation data; industry classifications are directly comparable for the published 2014-2026 window.
observations.uncertainty: Sector shares do not measure wages, scheduling, safety, retention, training, advancement, or the quality of the work experience; 2026 values use only June-July.
observations.subgroup: Employed teens ages 16 to 19 during summer months.
observations.counterinterpretation: Industry concentration may reflect seasonal demand and age eligibility rather than a durable narrowing of youth opportunity; sector movement does not prove a change in work socialization.

related_sources.claim: The Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey is the federal employment-data source analyzed by Pew.

boundary: This record adds a youth-work and socialization layer: teen summer employment has partly rebounded in 2026 but remains far below historical levels, varies sharply by age and race/ethnicity, and is concentrated in hospitality, retail, and logistics. It does not establish causes, earnings, job quality, school tradeoffs, household necessity, discrimination, or the long-term effect of early work exposure.
